title: Nepal lobbies for mountain agenda at COP31 - The Rising Nepal
description: Nepal lobbies for mountain agenda at COP31  The Rising Nepal
publisher.title: The Rising Nepal
full_article:
By A Staff Reporter

Kathmandu, Nov. 15: Minister for Foreign Affairs Shisir Khanal returned home on Saturday after leading the Nepali delegation to the 31st Conference of the Parties (COP31) to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), held in Antalya, Türkiye. The conference which started on November 9 will continue until November 20.

Minister Khanal had left for Antalya on November 7 following a decision of the Council of Ministers to participate in the conference. Minister for Agriculture, Forests and Environment Gita Chaudhary will lead the Nepali delegation during the final week of the conference and participate in scheduled meetings and negotiations, said a press statement issued by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs on Saturday.

The COP is one of the world’s major multilateral forums for setting common policies, commitments and directions to address global climate challenges and their impacts.

The conference, held annually since 1995, has placed particular stresses on limiting global temperature rise to 1.5 degrees Celsius, achieving net-zero carbon emissions by 2050, and strengthening the adaptive capacity and resilience of countries and communities affected by climate change.

The Nepali delegation has highlighted mountain and climate change issues under the UNFCCC process, maintaining the 1.5-degree Celsius target, protecting Himalayan ecosystems, climate justice, financial support for adaptation and loss and damage, strengthening multi-hazard early warning systems and mobilising international support for post-disaster reconstruction and recovery.

Nepal’s key engagements at COP31

Addressing the COP31 Opening Plenary on November 9, Foreign Minister Khanal drew the international community’s attention to the severe impacts of recent climate-induced disasters in Nepal on people’s lives, livelihoods, infrastructure and ecosystems.

He called for the establishment of a dedicated programme of work on mountains and climate change under COP31. He also stressed the need to maintain the 1.5-degree Celsius temperature goal, incorporate mountain-specific indicators into the frameworks of the Global Goal on Adaptation (GGA) and the New Collective Quantified Goal on Climate Finance (NCQG), and address the impacts of climate change from the mountains to the sea.

He also highlighted the need for international support to ensure swift and equitable post-disaster reconstruction in Nepal.

On November 10, Khanal addressed the Baku High-Level Dialogue on Adaptation on behalf of the Least Developed Countries (LDCs). Noting that LDCs, despite contributing little to climate change, bear a disproportionate share of its impacts, he said adaptation must be an integral part of climate justice.

Khanal, Chaudhary and other members of the Nepali delegation also attended the Antalya Leaders’ Summit on November 11. The summit was addressed by United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres and heads of state and government, ministers and senior officials from various countries.

Addressing the High-Level Event on Early Warning for All: Delivering on Our Promise to Protect Everyone on November 11, Khanal said effective early warning systems were essential to saving lives in mountain communities.

On November 12, Nepal, Bhutan, Kyrgyzstan, Pakistan and Tajikistan jointly organised a high-level event on advancing the mountain agenda. Addressing the event, Khanal said that when mountains are in crisis, humanity as a whole is in crisis. He called for bringing mountain issues from the margins to the centre of global climate negotiations.

He stressed the need for deep emission cuts, grant-based climate finance instead of loans, swift and equitable financial support for loss and damage, glacier monitoring, multi-hazard early warning systems and international recognition of mountain-related risks.

Nepal also organised a high-level side event on strengthening mountain resilience through adaptation finance in collaboration with Bhutan, Kyrgyzstan and international partners, including ICIMOD and Zoï

Environment Network.

On November 13, Khanal addressed an event on access to climate finance for Small Island Developing States (SIDS) and Least Developed Countries. He stressed the need to ensure predictable, accessible and grant-based climate finance to meet the needs of highly climate-vulnerable LDCs, Landlocked Developing Countries (LLDCs) and fragile high mountain ecosystems.

Nepal Pavilion and bilateral meetings

Khanal inaugurated the Nepal Pavilion at the COP31 venue on November 9. The pavilion provides a platform to showcase Nepal’s climate ambitions, achievements in biodiversity conservation and community-level climate adaptation initiatives to the international community.

During the conference, Khanal held separate meetings with Ethiopian Foreign Minister Gedion Timothewos, Finland’s Minister for Foreign Trade and Development Ville Tavio, and UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres. They discussed various issues of mutual interest and concern. He also held a group meeting with the UN Secretary-General alongside ministerial representatives of LDCs.

title: Opinion | Nepal’s psychedelic mushrooms need experts, not hype - The Kathmandu Post
description: Opinion | Nepal’s psychedelic mushrooms need experts, not hype  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
Two small brown mushrooms can look almost identical. One may contain psilocybin, a psychedelic compound now in late-stage clinical trials for treatment-resistant depression. The other may carry toxins that destroy the liver and even cause death. Telling them apart takes training, not a photograph on social media.

That distinction captures Nepal’s problem. Experts estimate that more than 30 Nepalis die each year after eating wild mushrooms, though no agency keeps an official count. Psychedelic mushrooms now add a new concern. A foreign drug-information site has billed Nepal as “Asia’s top psychedelic tourist destination”, and a mushroom website calls these fungi “not illegal yet”. What happens when shops selling them open in our tourist towns before the regulator or the expert arrives? I have found no published data on how widespread use has become. We risk drifting towards a psychedelic market without ever deciding to have one.

As a physician-scientist who studies classic psychedelics and their health effects, I see neither miracle nor menace. I see a potent pharmacological tool, a country with a genuine opportunity, and a shortage of what makes that tool safe: expert knowledge backed by legal authority.

A drug shaped by its context

Psilocybin is the active compound in so-called magic mushrooms. One major review counts 144 hallucinogenic species in the genus Psilocybe alone. Psilocybin is a prodrug: the body converts it into psilocin, which acts chiefly on serotonin 2A receptors and can, for several hours, profoundly alter perception, emotion and the sense of self. Unusually, in medicine, outcomes appear to depend not only on molecule and dose but on the person’s state of mind and surroundings, i.e., set and setting. Clinical protocols therefore surround each dose with screening, preparation, monitoring and follow-up.

Promise, read critically

Compass Pathways has reported two phase 3 trials of synthetic psilocybin for treatment-resistant depression. In the first, a single 25 mg dose outperformed placebo by 3.6 points on a standard depression scale at six weeks. In the second, 39 percent of patients given two 25 mg doses improved by at least 25 percent, on average sustaining that benefit through week 26. Smaller studies suggest possible benefits in cancer-related distress and alcohol use disorder, and research extends to post-traumatic stress and obsessive-compulsive disorders, where evidence remains preliminary.

Scepticism remains a scientific duty. These results are company-reported, and the 3.6-point difference is modest. Because participants can usually tell whether they received a psychedelic, blinding often fails and placebo comparisons can mislead. A March 2026 meta-analysis in the Journal of the American Medical Association (JAMA) Psychiatry, drawing on only eight psychedelic trials, found psychedelic therapy no more effective than antidepressants taken by patients who knew what they were receiving.

Nor do these findings transfer to a bag of dried mushrooms. Trials give screened patients an exact dose of a purified compound. A 2025 review in JAMA Psychiatry warned that such results do not generalise to public use, and cited more than 20-fold differences in potency among mushroom samples. Psilocybe cubensis is easy to grow at home, so informal supply can spread quickly.

Where the harm lies

Psilocybin has relatively low physical toxicity, which makes its risks easy to underestimate. Documented dangers include agitation, confusion, a racing heart, and psychiatric destabilisation, particularly in people with a personal or family history of psychotic symptoms, whom most psychedelic trials exclude. A recent preprint from licensed services in Oregon and Colorado, not yet peer-reviewed, reported large short-term improvements but flagged possible risk of increased suicidality. That signal matters in Nepal, where 6.5 percent of adults in the national survey reported current suicidal thoughts.

Nepal adds a hazard that trials never measure: misidentification. Studies count 1,291 wild mushroom species here, more than 100 of them poisonous. Some deadly Galerina species resemble psilocybin mushrooms while carrying the same toxins as the death cap. Symptoms may appear only after many hours, and our health posts are poorly equipped for severe poisoning. Someone seeking a spiritual experience could end up with liver failure.

The Narcotic Drugs (Control) Act, 1976 does not name psilocybin, but covers any psychotropic substance the government specifies in the Nepal Gazette. Its status is therefore unclear, and silence is not permission.

The expertise already here

Nepal need not import all the knowledge it requires. During my recent visit to Nepal, I spent some time with Tikaram Aryal, president of the Himalayan Mushroom firm in Pokhara, who holds a master’s degree in plant science and has 25 years of experience in mycology. In my assessment, he is an expert on psilocybin mushrooms, and precisely the kind of Nepali specialist any serious policy discussion should include. Such expertise needs a formal channel to inform the state.

Mycological and medical expertise must also meet. A mycologist can establish what a mushroom is, and how to grow it consistently. A clinician can judge who should not take it, and manage what goes wrong. License and authority to cultivate, distribute, and guide should rest with experienced, vetted experts in these fields, and with no one else.

Nepal’s opportunity

Under such a framework, this could benefit the country. Nepal is a natural paradise, with Himalayan landscapes, rich fungal diversity, and deep traditions of meditation and healing. More than 1.15 million foreign tourists visited Nepal in 2025 alone. Licensed psychedelic retreats, offering screening, guided sessions, and follow-up, could attract visitors who stay longer and spend more. In Jamaica, week-long retreats were charging $2,300 to$10,500 per person as early as 2020.

But ‘retreat’ guarantees nothing. A January study in JAMA Network Open examined 49 retreat organisations and found wide variation in safety practices. A session in a remote valley, hours from a hospital, is a liability. Nepal should compete on safety, not permissiveness.

Revenue needs an explicit model. The state could collect annual license fees from cultivators, laboratories, retreat centres, and guides, plus a tax on each supervised session. A fixed share should fund public mental health services, since official 2020 data counted only about 200 psychiatrists in Nepal, and retreats must not draw them away from Nepali patients. Projections should stay sober: Oregon taxes psilocybin products at 15 percent, yet regulators there projected a two-year shortfall of about $3.8 million without higher fees.

Exports are a longer-term prospect. Psilocybin sits in the strictest schedule of the 1971 UN Convention on Psychotropic Substances. The mushrooms themselves are not listed, leaving each government to decide, and many control them nationally. Article 32’s exception for wild plants covers only small groups’ traditional rites, and not international trade, so it offers no shortcut. The realistic market is therefore tested, with research-grade material shipped under permits to authorised laboratories. A company has reported exporting about 20 kg from Jamaica to Canada for clinical trial production. Nepal should first document its native strains and secure benefit-sharing for its communities.

What the government must do

None of this will happen without government support. Working with the tourism, agriculture, and commerce ministries, the Ministry of Health and Population should focus on the following:

Clarify and inform: Settle the legal status, stop unlicensed sales, and launch an expert-led public campaign on risks, benefits, and myths. Convene experts: Bring together mycologists, physicians, pharmacologists, toxicologists, lawyers, and community representatives. Build the science: Create a licensed research window, with ethics review by the Nepal Health Research Council. Fund species surveys, potency testing, and training in controlled cultivation. Educate health professionals: Doctors, nurses, and pharmacists need training on benefits, contraindications, drug interactions, and emergency care. License experienced experts: Require tested batches, medical screening, informed consent, and mandatory adverse event reporting, and revoke licenses for breaches.

title: Opinion | AI is coming to Nepal either way. The real question is who’s in charge - The Kathmandu Post
description: Opinion | AI is coming to Nepal either way. The real question is who’s in charge  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
Last month, Nepal took government systems offline to patch two critical PHP flaws, a reminder that sovereignty starts with knowing what we run and being able to change it. The stakes extend well beyond government servers. Technological advancements have reshaped how we live, interact and communicate. The most pervasive technology of our times is AI, which is now integral to business, administration, innovation, and almost all human function. Its importance can be gauged from the fact that today the question for countries worldwide is not whether to implement AI but to implement in a way to serve national interests without compromising autonomy and sovereignty.

AI in Nepal can be a gateway to progress and prosperity, ensuring equitable access to education and enabling businesses, specifically small and mid-sized enterprises, to compete in the global market. This said, technology needs to be implemented responsibly in a way that the country retains its sovereignty and doesn’t become subservient to foreign-controlled data and systems. Technological independence is therefore extremely important. This does not imply building technology from scratch but forging foreign partnerships that help build local capabilities without encroaching on sensitive data and systems. Thus, Nepal must be able to govern the AI it buys—it must retain the ability to choose, govern, and adapt technologies to align with its unique needs while also having complete control over data and decision-making.

Building capacity, securing control

The country has already taken concrete steps in this direction, the foremost being introducing the National Artificial Intelligence Policy, 2025, which sets the guidelines for AI use in Nepal, with the aim of leveraging technology for research, innovation, and business and administrative support, while addressing all data and related issues to promote national interests. It has also received a $50 million loan from the World Bank to support the Nepal Digital Transformation Project, and another $90 million from the Asian Development Bank for strengthening the digital infrastructure needed to effectively implement the technology.

However, these investments must not undermine Nepal’s ability to independently control, monitor and audit its AI systems. This is in line with the OECD's Digital Government Outlook 2026, which reiterates that public institutions must ensure accountability and transparency, maintain data rights and manage lifecycle risks. Thus, to manage the technology it buys, Nepal must develop local talent, institutional capacities, and frameworks to retain control and safeguard its technological autonomy.

The need for technological autonomy

Technological autonomy is crucial in that while AI may improve efficiency and save time, integrating it with proprietary software may expose sensitive data to external entities, posing a significant data breach. Thus, while acquiring AI technology, it’s extremely crucial to address relevant questions, more specifically in terms of who retains control over records, who audits the systems, and what contingency measures are in place in case the service is compromised or becomes unavailable. These concerns must be addressed before and not after technology acquisition and implementation because it’s less expensive to fix issues at the outset than when they are entrenched in the systems.

Preserving Nepal’s rich heritage

Data security and technological autonomy apart, the new AI systems must align with Nepal’s rich cultural and linguistic heritage. While most global models adapt well to Nepali, performance may vary across dialects and even some public sector contexts. This problem can be resolved by investing in translation resources, Nepali-language datasets, digitised public archives, and evaluation benchmarks. Domestic companies and Universities too can build the necessary tools that preserve our rich heritage and independently evaluate if imported systems meet local needs without simply relying on the vendors’ claims. For instance, Kathmandu University’s language lab has undertaken a project to build a Nepali- Tamang and English translation system and benchmarked global multilingual models on its own data instead of relying on claims.

Building capabilities

First, Nepal needs to build its digital infrastructure, data, and skills, aligned with the UNCTAD's Technology and Innovation Report 2025, which sets the guidelines for public institutions on how to govern and share data through external systems, and who is accountable for its use. Second, the country must build domestic skills and capabilities to reduce dependence on external vendors to preserve national autonomy while also ensuring preservation of its rich cultural and linguistic heritage. Third, contracts with overseas vendors should include provisions for interoperability, auditability, data portability, exit options and future maintenance expenses. Although relying on one vendor may lower upfront costs, it could become expensive over time by reducing both switching options and bargaining power. Fourth, there is a need for clear safeguards for agentic AI with restricted access, audit logs, and designated approval for major decisions. Before deployments, pilot systems should first be tested for accuracy, security, bias, and failure risks. Fifth, there is also a need to appropriately measure outcomes in terms of the use of domestic talent and open Nepali-language resources to gauge whether the country is actually retaining technological autonomy or simply producing documents.

Sovereignty is not isolation

title: Opinion | Is Nepali politics forgetting its own history? - The Kathmandu Post
description: Opinion | Is Nepali politics forgetting its own history?  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
Seeking a path of action in history is a serious subject. Nepal is going through a process of retrospection and introspection in matters of political processes and experiments. We are also facing the double whammy of ecology and economy today. Tackling with a strange mix of natural calamity and political experiments is not a smooth process to go through for a country like Nepal. That demands a high degree of dedication, honesty and openness on all fronts. The dominant metaphors that are rife today are political in nature. Other issues of morality, conspiracy, intrigue, and even the open use of post-truth practices mark the most challenging and intriguing moment in history that people are experiencing today. It is a debatable question—when do the events become historical, and when are we able to see and review them? We have to seek solutions to all problems through our own mechanisms. I take the example of politics in this essay.

A few very debatable and what appear to be the crucial questions in Nepali politics have struck me in recent times. That makes it a more interesting, challenging and sometimes inspiring subject for anyone who wants to understand the present texture of politically defined society. The reason for my own interest in this subject is shaped like this. I am neither a dabbler in politics nor has it ever become a subject of preoccupation. But as an academic with literature, cultural studies and art as the principal topics of engagement and pedagogical practice, the concept of politics comes to lodge with me as a subject imbued with the meaning charged with the spirit of presentism, to use a philosophical term. Nepali politics and the little unsettled and ongoing sense of history make me evoke this philosophy. It seems, despite a pretty long history and experiments with ideologies, that contemporary Nepali politics is shaped by presentism. That is to say, the thrust of all Nepali political discourses and concerns is shaped by the tides of presentism. For that reason, I simply want to allude to the gist of this philosophy in a few words.

According to the concept of presentism, only the objects that exist now are real. The past is also important, but the history and the future should be judged from the present. I feel inundated by presentism in Nepal because it seems our discussions and interactions are shaped by what is happening now, and not by what happened yesterday and what may happen in the future. The claims are interesting. Nepali political parties and ideologies mostly use a few metaphors and themes of history. What I find interesting is that the Nepali political parties have inadvertently made the important themes of history, mostly of Western origin, the principal guidelines of their actions. They include Marxism, liberalism, democracy, humanism with rights as the focus, and an independent judiciary.

What is remarkable is that in a short period of time, Nepali political parties and their architects have made experiments with the principal themes of history. The above themes constitute the philosophy of discussions among the Nepali politicians and thinkers. The political and historical aspects of this subject is remarkably discussed by scholars and media analysts. I have read some works of academics like Lok Raj Baral, his erstwhile students Krishna Khanal and Krishna Hachethyu, and historians like Triratna Manandhar, Pratyoush Onta and John Whelpton. The works of earlier historians like Rishikesh Shah, Leo Rose and Bhuvan Lal Joshi are helpful readings. There is no dearth of cogently presented interpretations by writers in Nepali printed media, online portals and podcasts run by experienced media people.

One other thing should be mentioned here. The political parties themselves have developed an interest in interpreting some aspects of the major schools of thought and the trends in politics. That involves the personas and the writings and rhetoric of the leaders of the political parties they represent. The political leaders of the parties took up the cudgel of interpreting current political situations through their manifestos. What is interesting is that the political parties made political ideologies the guiding principles of their actions. There is a history of that. BP Koirala and his party adopted a philosophy of social democracy with liberal ideas, a multiparty system and an independent judiciary as guiding principles and ethics. Socialism was considered the goal of the political party that we find enshrined in the writings of BP Koirala, Ganesh Man Singh, and Krishna Prasad Bhattarai. Their successors appear to reiterate those principles, some brilliantly, and others very poorly. The communists use Marxist lingo in their political discourses more than any other political parties. The volume of Marxist-Leninist principles is quite large in their discourses. The Maoists used the concept of revolution in a classical sense.

The political parties of different orders meet on the concept of democracy. One example is here. The Maoists, after coming out of the jungle in 2006, entered politics known under the nomenclature of democracy espoused by the 'seven' major political parties and their leaders in Nepal. A short reference is eloquent. Hindustan Tim e s , in its news of November 18, 2006, quoted the Maoist leader Prachanda as saying at the Hindustan Times conference in Delhi, "I have lived my life in the jungle; now I will lead my life in light". Prachanda and Girija Prasad Koirala signed the Comprehensive Peace Agreement after a week on 26 November. The paper further writes, "Nepal's firebrand Maoist leader Prachanda on Saturday said the political battle in the 21st century will be fought over democracy, which at present is in deep crisis." It is interesting to see the Maoist guerrilla leader showing anxiety over the crisis faced by democracy. The newspaper Kantipur of 20 November 2006 reported former Indian prime ministers VP Singh and I.K. Gujral calling Prachanda as one who was representing to them the archetype of a revolutionary read in history books.

title: NT’s net profit rises by 37.35% in Q1 - The Rising Nepal
description: NT’s net profit rises by 37.35% in Q1  The Rising Nepal
publisher.title: The Rising Nepal
full_article:
By A Staff Reporter

Kathmandu, Nov. 15: Nepal Telecom (NT) has recorded a 37.35 per cent year-on-year increase in net profit to Rs. 1.82 billion in the first quarter of the current fiscal year 2026/27.

According to the company's unaudited financial statement, its net profit stood at Rs. 1.32 billion in the corresponding period of the previous fiscal year.

The company's profit before tax also increased by 3.65 per cent to Rs. 2.98 billion from Rs. 2.88 billion in the same period last fiscal year.

However, its earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation (EBITDA) declined by 6.13 per cent to Rs. 4.45 billion from Rs. 4.75 billion.

The company reported total operating income of Rs. 8.67 billion during the review period, almost unchanged from Rs. 8.67 billion in the corresponding period of the previous fiscal year.

Its total income increased slightly to Rs. 9.47 billion from Rs. 9.47 billion.

Nepal Telecom attributed the changes in its revenue and profit to disruptions caused by floods and landslides in different parts of the country, increased employee expenses and changes in operating costs.

The company said it provided free voice and data services to customers affected by the devastating floods and landslides in the Bhotekoshi area of Rasuwa for 17 days from August 26.

The disaster also disrupted telecommunication services and commercial activities in the affected areas, reducing service sales and revenue. The floods in the Budhigandaki area on October 11 also affected its services.

The company said the increasing use of large-volume mobile data packages at lower prices had also influenced its operating revenue. Revenue from GSM and FTTH services increased by Rs. 1.016 million and Rs. 44 million, respectively.

Despite an increase in employee expenses following a salary scale adjustment, the company's net expenses declined by Rs. 481.2 million, or 5.90 per cent, due to lower depreciation expenses and impairment reversal adjustments.

Nepal Telecom said it had continued prioritising service expansion and quality improvement even in remote and geographically challenging areas where operating costs are high and returns are relatively low.

KATHMANDU, Nov 15: Nepal and India are expected to revive discussions on accelerating the long-delayed Pancheshwar Multipurpose Project during Prime Minister Balen Shah’s upcoming state visit to India, beginning November 22.

The proposed project is likely to be one of five key issues on the agenda for bilateral talks, according to government officials. Indian media have also quoted Uttarakhand Cabinet Minister Satpal Maharaj as confirming that the Pancheshwar project will be discussed during the Nepali prime minister’s visit.

Related story APF border out post established at Pancheshwar

Preparations are underway in Uttarakhand for the proposed visit. Indian media, citing Minister Maharaj, reported that the discussions will also cover cross-border trade, infrastructure development, including a proposed dry port in Mahendranagar, and tourism promotion in Nepal’s Terai region.

Located on the Mahakali River, the Pancheshwar Multipurpose Project is one of the most significant joint infrastructure initiatives between Nepal and India. Despite its strategic importance, the project has made little progress over the past several decades due to disagreements over investment costs, water allocation and benefit-sharing.

The project was envisaged under the 1996 Mahakali Treaty, with the objectives of generating hydropower, providing irrigation facilities and controlling floods in both countries. Its implementation is expected to unlock substantial hydropower potential while strengthening bilateral cooperation in water resource development.

In recent years, both countries have stepped up efforts to finalize the project's Detailed Project Report (DPR). They have reportedly narrowed their differences over construction costs, with discussions indicating that Nepal would contribute around 25–30 percent of the total investment, while India would finance the remainder.

However, an agreement on sharing the benefits derived from the Mahakali River remains elusive. This unresolved issue continues to be a major obstacle to finalizing the project and moving towards implementation.

publisher.title: The Rising Nepal
full_article:
By Lilaraj Khadka

Jhapa, Nov. 15: Rivers and ponds across Jhapa have been beautifully decorated for the Chhath festival, with local residents contributing their labour to prepare the riverbanks for the celebrations.

The banks of the Mechi and Kankai Mai rivers, which lie along the Nepal-India border, have taken on a festive look as devotees from both countries come together to celebrate the festival, adding to its charm.

Preparations for Chhath, which follows the Dashain and Tihar festivals, began a week in advance, with local residents working together to decorate riverbanks and ponds. Devotees have been observing the festival at more than a dozen rivers and ponds across the district, including the Biring, Kankai Mai, Ratuwa, Andhuwa, Ninda and Mechi rivers.

Chhath celebration committees said that devotees would stay awake throughout Sunday night at the Kankai Mai and Biring riverbanks. The celebrations will also feature Ganga Aarti and musical performances by national artists.

This year, preparations are under way to organise Chhath celebrations on a grand scale at the Biring River in Kankai Municipality. The organisers shared details of the preparations at a press conference.

As there is insufficient space to construct worship platforms along the Andhuwa stream in Birtamod, devotees from the area have been visiting the Biring River to perform Chhath rituals for the past few years.

The Chhath Samaj Sewa Samiti, Birtamod, said it was preparing to organise the festival in a well-managed and grand manner at the Biring River, as in previous years. According to the committee's chairperson, Sangeeta Rauniyar, 190 worship platforms have been constructed this year, with space for two devotees at each platform.

At a press meet held in Birtamod on Friday, the committee briefed the media on its preparations. Committee secretary Jay Kumar Jha said a main organising committee had been formed under the coordination of Shankar Bhagat to oversee the celebrations. Chairperson Rauniyar said various subcommittees had also been formed and responsibilities assigned to ensure the smooth conduct of the festival.

Meanwhile, preparations have also been completed to make the traditional Chhath celebrations along the Kankai River more organised, said Khagendra Mahato, chairperson of the Kankai Chhath Puja Committee. He said the programme would include an overnight vigil, cultural performances and Ganga Aarti on Sunday.

Similarly, devotees from both Nepal and India will gather along the Mechi River at Bhadrapur-5 for the celebrations. Bhadrapur Municipality Mayor Ganesh Pokharel said an overnight vigil and Ganga Aarti would also be organised there.

According to the programme, devotees will offer prayers to the setting sun on Sunday evening and conclude the festival by offering arghya to the rising sun on Monday morning.

title: Protecting peace with pictures - Nepali Times
description: Protecting peace with pictures  Nepali Times
publisher.title: Nepali Times
full_article:
A mushroom cloud rising over Hiroshima after the US dropped an atom bomb on the city in 1945. Children fleeing a US napalm attack on a Vietnamese village in 1972. A lone man carrying shopping bags standing in front of a line of tanks on Tiananmen Square in 1989. Passengers lying dead in the aftermath of a Maoist ambush of a passenger bus in Chitwan in 2005. Children desperately extending utensils in the hope of recieving aid amid the genocide in Gaza.

The history of violence, conflict, and genocide across the world is well documented and ingrained in the global consciousness. But what comes to mind when people are told to conjure an image of peace?

The foreword of Tiffany Fairey’s new book Imaging Peace, asks this very question, leaving the reader to ponder. Unlike imagery of violent events, photos of peace are passive symbols – a V sign, a dove, an olive branch, a dove carrying an olive branch.

One could argue that depicting peace has limitations. After all, in the absence of violence, don’t all photographs depict peace? But in societies which have faced wars, conflicts, and genocide, peace is not a foregone conclusion, it needs to be built and protected. The end of war does not automatically mean peace.

This is where peace photography comes in.

COUNTER ARCHIVE

Fairey’s book looks at various methods of the visual documentation of peace in six countries which have faced armed conflicts, genocide, and violent events: in Colombia, Rwanda, Nepal, Northern Ireland, Mexico, as well as Bosnia and Herzgovina.

The approaches include photovoice, photo mentorship, therapeutic and participatory photography, and in the case of Nepal, visual archives that focus directly on the memory and aftermath of the decade-long Maoist conflict.

The Nepal chapter looks at post-conflict visual documentation by three collectives in the aftermath of the decade-long Maoist insurgency: a trilogy of books and travelling exhibitions titled A People War, Never Again, and People After War led by journalist Kunda Dixit, who is the publisher of Nepali Times, The Feminist Memory project initiated by the Nepal Picture Library, and Memory, Truth and Justice, of Voices of Women (VOW) media.

The case studies are examples of a 'counter archive', a component of peace photography which subverts established historical accounts and creates space for previously sidelined and intersectional stories to be shared.

Through travelling exhibitions and books, the initiatives allowed what began as a collection of photographs to evolve into testimonies, facilitating discourse and ultimately helping healing.

Fairey argues that in Nepal, like elsewhere in the world, historical archives are repositories of power structures, and archival practices have served to uphold dominant historical narratives of the decade-long conflict while excluding ‘marginalised and plural histories’.

‘Such archives not only establish and legitimise hidden and revised histories, but by making them visible they work to activate and build public and political imaginaries,’ writes Fairey.

Photo: NEPAL PICTURE LIBRARY

One of the women featured in the Feminist Memory project is Ashmita Khadka. In an archival image, Khadka is smiling at the camera (pictured, above) with her hair wrapped in a towel as she kneels in the snow, happy because to wash after many days.

title: Call For Climate Justice - The Rising Nepal
description: Call For Climate Justice  The Rising Nepal
publisher.title: The Rising Nepal
full_article:
The 31st Conference of the Parties (COP31) to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) kicked off on Monday in Antalya, Türkiye, with 196 countries and the European Union attending to discuss the global climate crisis. For least developed countries like Nepal, the global climate summit is more than a diplomatic gathering. It is an important platform to demand climate justice, secure adequate financial resources and draw international attention to the growing threats facing the Himalayas.

Standing alongside other Global South nations, Nepal has emerged as a vocal advocate for climate justice, calling on wealthy, high-emitting countries to scale up climate finance and provide dedicated funding to address loss and damage in vulnerable regions. From the beginning, the Nepali delegation has asked to put mountain issues at the centre of global climate discussions. They also highlighted how rising temperatures, melting glaciers and increasingly extreme weather events are threatening Himalayan ecosystems and the communities dependent on them. Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal addressed the COP31 Opening Plenary. He highlighted the devastating impacts of recent climate-induced disasters in Nepal, primarily the Bhotekoshi flood on August 26, which many have described as a “Himalayan Tsunami”. He also inaugurated the Nepal Pavilion, which showcases the country's biodiversity conservation efforts and community-based adaptation initiatives.

While negotiators at COP31 debate climate finance, emission reductions and the responsibilities of developed nations, communities in Nepal continue to struggle with the effects of climate-induced disasters. The Bhotekoshi disaster has demonstrated how vulnerable mountain communities are to sudden and destructive events. Nepal estimates that it needs more than US$4.7 billion for recovery and reconstruction. Such a huge financial burden could push the country further into debt, despite its negligible contribution to historical global emissions. Last month, the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage approved US$20 million under its funding arrangements. However, this amount is far below the country's recovery needs and several procedural steps must still be completed before Nepal can access the funds.

Minister for Agriculture, Forest and Environment Gita Chaudhary, who took over leadership of Nepal's delegation following Khanal's return to Kathmandu on Saturday, presented the “Living Sagarmatha: Nepal Himalayan Resilience Strategy”, seeking to bring cryosphere and forest management under a common resilience framework. Nepal and Bhutan have also pushed for Himalayan issues from the beginning to receive greater recognition in formal climate negotiations. Although their proposal has gained limited reception in the formal agenda, efforts to advance the mountain agenda are continuing. Nepal must therefore continue advocating for a dedicated UNFCCC programme of work on mountains and mountain-specific indicators in global adaptation and climate finance goals. Mountain ecosystems cannot remain a marginal issue when their degradation has costs far beyond national borders.

The signing of a Framework Agreement for Cooperation on Climate Change between Nepal and the Republic of Korea on Friday is a positive step towards strengthening bilateral cooperation in carbon finance, emission reductions, climate resilience and sustainable development. Cooperation under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement could create opportunities for climate-friendly investment and technology transfer, provided that environmental integrity and national interests remain protected. Nepal's presence at COP31 must go beyond highlighting its vulnerability. It must translate into concrete commitments, predictable and accessible grant-based finance, technology transfer and stronger international cooperation. Developed countries must recognise their responsibility and ensure that climate finance reaches the communities on the front lines of the crisis. For Nepal, climate justice should not remain a slogan repeated at international conferences, it must become tangible support for people whose lives, livelihoods and future are increasingly threatened by a crisis they did little to create.

title: Why Nepal's Democracy Falters - The Rising Nepal
description: Why Nepal's Democracy Falters  The Rising Nepal
publisher.title: The Rising Nepal
full_article:
The lofty political ideals incorporated in the constitution become repetitive clichés when governance becomes eternally dysfunctional. A yawning gap between the promises and delivery only triggers another cycle of frustration and rebellion. The people are condemned to bear the Sisyphus fate and act as mere means of enforcing procedural democracy propped up by cosmetic reforms devoid of substance, hope and conviction. If one goes through democratic upheavals and their faulty practices in Nepal spanning over seven decades, a painful scenario pounds us. We confront the discourses on the failure of democracy and promised governance.

However, contextual realities and cultural diversity are often ignored while decoding the inherent contradictions that hasten the decline of democratic polity. Are democratic values universal or nation-specific? Former South Korean president Kim Dae-jung and Singaporean leader Lee Kuan Yew engaged in a classic debate over this question. Dae-jung often argued that democracy contains universal virtues but Lee dismissed the Western-style liberal democracy as the universal model of development. The logic of both statesmen carries a certain ounce of truth. But experience has shown that a one-size-fits-all approach to democracy does not work. If so, the third-world countries would have attained prosperity and democratic maturity; many of them followed the prescriptions of Western ideas and prescriptions on establishing democracy, human rights and economic growth.

Industrial revolution

For centuries, the powerful Western nations colonised many countries in Asia and Africa. The resources extracted from the colonised countries, combined with domestic technological breakthroughs and cheap labour, fuelled the Industrial Revolution in Britain in the 18th and 19th centuries, while slavery was considered a catalytic force in American industrial development. These industrial revolutions, considered brutal, gave rise to the labour movement, and notions of political parties, and civil and democratic struggles. Watching the struggle between the working class and the capitalist one, Marx developed communist theory that contains a set of ideologies: class struggle, dialectical materialism, surplus value, theory of alienation and false consciousness. Marx says, “Democracy is the road to socialism.” But his deterministic theory and attempts to universalise Western-born communism could not be successfully applied to other parts of the world, though it inspired millions of people to rise in revolt against injustice and exploitation.

Blind imitation of ideology ends in catastrophe, for it underestimates the historical and cultural evolution of given nations. Visionary leaders do not copy other ideas but contextualise them. For instance, Mao indigenised Marxism and refused to toe the line of Stalin during the Chinese Civil War. Practical insights have guided China to bolster its soft power in the world. This is a reason it has promoted Confucianism for this purpose.

If one makes a deep review of Nepali democracy and the communist movement, it gives an unambiguous conclusion: market and communist fundamentalism are unsustainable and disastrous for the people. The growth model prescribed by the Bretton Woods institutions such as the IMF and World Bank has abysmally failed. Today, our youth do not see a future at home. The manufacturing base is so weak that the country does not have industries that have an edge in the international market. If the privatisation of public enterprises were right, why are there no vibrant industries capable of absorbing around 500,000 people entering the labour market annually? The remittance-based and import-driven economy is vulnerable to internal and external shocks. Our precarious economy debunks the theory of trickle-down prosperity.

So is liberal democracy, which is increasingly becoming illiberal and unsocial. Western democracy is unable to satisfy its own people. Currently, they are revolting against the elected leaders over the shabby education infrastructure, rising living costs, and inequality. The liberal order is in rapid decline, with an alternative global order gradually taking shape. But Nepal still follows an outdated economic model that runs counter to the constitution.

Bellicose movement

In the mid-1990s, Nepal witnessed a bellicose Maoist insurgency that was an attempt to force communist fundamentalism in the country. Its proponents claim that the movement enabled the nation to attain some far-reaching political rights. However, the insurgency also met the interests of the external elements determined to maintain ‘controlled instability’ in the Himalayan nation. It tried to vilify the nation’s founding father, the national unification campaign and damage the harmonious native culture, an umbilical cord that unites the Nepali people.

It has been more than three and a half decades since Nepal experimented with democracy. ‘Democracy’ is the most popular, vibrant and bold term that the members of the public use as a weapon against the tyrants, arrogant and corrupt leaders. It requires true democrats to make democracy a successful project. The leaders who win the popular mandate must learn to respect the democratic ethos and constitutional norms. Democracy involves both process and content. Gandhi was right when he said only the correct means lead to desired outcomes. He stood against the argument that the end justifies the means. A credible and transparent means yields sustainable results acceptable to a broader spectrum of politics. But corrupt and arrogant politicians are afraid of embracing this playbook of democracy, inviting the civil unrest that costs unnecessary lives and property. In such a milieu, democracy falters and the public loses confidence in democratic politics. Thus, the citizens must wake up to tame the insensitive politicians who use the electoral mandate as a fig leaf to hide their dark side and serve vested interests.

(The author is the Managing Editor of this daily.)

publisher.title: OnlineKhabar English News
full_article:
Antalya (Türkiye), November 15

Minister for Agriculture, Forests and Environment Gita Chaudhary held a bilateral meeting with Global Green Growth Institute (GGGI) Executive Director Sang-Hyup Kim on the sidelines of the ongoing COP31 climate conference in Antalya, Türkiye, on Saturday.

The two discussed ways to strengthen cooperation in climate finance and green development, particularly to support climate-vulnerable communities and promote sustainable growth.

The meeting also focused on Nepal’s priorities and potential areas for future collaboration.

During the meeting, Chaudhary acknowledged GGGI’s support for Nepal in areas including climate-friendly agriculture, clean transportation, green finance and ecosystem restoration.

Emphasising the need to make the partnership more strategic and institutional, she said COP31 provided an important opportunity for mountainous and climate-vulnerable countries to secure adequate access to climate finance and investment.

Highlighting the contribution of GGGI-supported climate-friendly agriculture projects to farming and employment, Chaudhary called for expanded cooperation to help farmers cope with the impacts of climate change.

She also stressed the need to promote climate-resilient farming, improve weather monitoring systems and develop sustainable agricultural value chains to strengthen farmers’ capacity to adapt to climate change.

GGGI Executive Director Kim expressed his willingness to expand cooperation with Nepal in these areas.
